leading_positions.synthesis: Four of eight members prefer optical lattice clocks, all with the same two names (Katori, Ye) and a citation built on magic-wavelength lattice clocks reaching about 1e-18. They share the view that the attribution is compact, the result has been independently reproduced and compared across laboratories, and the interpretation is stable. They do not fully share a view on credit: Olsson and Kroll want the Katori/Ye boundary and the claims of Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and Takamoto checked against the primary record, whereas Lindroth does not regard those contributors as a reason for a third name. Johansson and Olsson changed their first choice after reading the opening ballots, and Olsson cites a conflict on her earlier top choice as a reason for the move. All four name the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as the main reservation, and the pending redefinition of the second as a secondary one.

Eriksson alone prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer), as a quantitative prediction followed by experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states, reproduced by independent groups. Eriksson accepts that the pairing mechanism is open and argues the prize would be for the phases, not the mechanism. Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson list it as an alternative, but Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson cite maturity, sample dependence, and the omission of Cao as reasons to wait.

Mehlig alone prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), arguing the mechanism is identified and well understood after more than a decade of independent confirmation. Eriksson lists it as an alternative. Mehlig concedes that the 2016 topological-phases prize and the claims of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan are open issues.

Danielsson alone prefers the Higgs boson discovery at ATLAS and CMS, with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, on the grounds of scale of consequence and a decade of confirmation. Danielsson concedes that the shortlisted credited set includes Della Negra, who is omitted from the preferred names, and that attribution is the hardest on the list. Pearce lists B019 as an alternative but says he cannot see a defensible three-name set; Johansson stresses the attribution cost of a collaboration prize.

Pearce (chair) alone prefers IceCube (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) as a new observational window. Danielsson lists it as an alternative. Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson explicitly respond that attribution (AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND lineage) and maturity of source-level evidence are unsettled, and Pearce himself records both reservations.

areas_of_agreement: Optical lattice clocks (B059) are the only candidate ranked in the preferred configuration by a plurality of members (four of eight), and all four use the same two names; Danielsson, Pearce and Eriksson list it as an alternative, so seven of eight members either prefer it or list it as an alternative in round 1; Mehlig, whose preference is B016, describes the clock case as clean and strongly supported, but does not list it as an alternative.

Every member prefers a single-part prize with a three-name cap or less; no member proposes a two-part prize in round 1, although Olsson asks whether a method prize could be considered later alongside B059.

Members agree that the physics of the Higgs boson, twisted bilayer graphene, topological insulators, IceCube and circuit QED is real; the disagreements concern attribution, maturity and overlap with earlier prizes, not whether the observations are secure.
Several members (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson) state that circuit QED (B013) faces a distinctness problem after the 2025 prize and that Girvin and Devoret are outside the credited trio.
Members agree that any citation for B059 must rest on the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself rather than on the frequency comb or on optical clocks in general.
scientific_disputes: Whether optical lattice clocks are a distinct discovery or a refinement of the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control work (raised by Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson, Mehlig and Pearce).

Whether the pairing mechanism and sample dependence in twisted bilayer graphene undermine the discovery of correlated and superconducting phases, or only their detailed phase diagram (Eriksson against Johansson, Lindroth, Kroll, Mehlig, Olsson, Danielsson).

Whether the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux alone constitutes a prize-worthy discovery, given that individual source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are at modest significance and KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD confirmation is still developing (Pearce, Kroll, Olsson).
Whether the Higgs discovery, as a finished discovery of nature, outweighs the cleaner attribution of other candidates (Danielsson against Johansson).

Whether circuit QED is a new physical discovery after the 2025 prize or an enabling architecture, with the transmon and device engineering responsible for much of the impact (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Pearce, Olsson).
attribution_disputes: B059: Katori and Ye are named by every member who proposes laureates, but Olsson and Kroll ask whether Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto or others have a claim, and Olsson asks whether the proposal and first strontium demonstrations are Katori's while Ye's contribution is performance and many-body clock physics; Lindroth and Johansson ask whether Ye's credit is for the lattice clock or partly for the already honoured comb work.

B019: the shortlisted credited set is Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, but Danielsson's preferred three omit Della Negra; Danielsson, Pearce and Johansson question whether any three names would reflect scientific decisions rather than collaboration leadership roles.

B043: Pearce's preferred names (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) differ from the pair Halzen and Karle in some opening proposals, and Olsson and Lindroth question the decisive roles of the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leaders.
B034: Cao and Fatemi, first experimentalists, and Dean's and Young's groups are outside the credited names (Eriksson, Danielsson, Lindroth, Olsson).
B016: Mele is a co-author of the Kane-Mele paper, while Hasan and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the preferred three (Mehlig, Mehlig, Danielsson, Eriksson).
B013: Girvin and Devoret are outside the credited trio, and the Yale, Delft and Zurich lines overlap (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson).
maturity_disputes: Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second is a reason to wait or a sign of maturity for B059 (Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson, Johansson, Pearce).
Whether eight years is enough for twisted bilayer graphene, with Eriksson arguing the phases are reproduced and Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Kroll and Danielsson arguing for waiting.
Whether IceCube's source-level results are mature enough for the astrophysical interpretation (Pearce, Kroll, Olsson).
Whether 2025 proximity is a reason to delay circuit QED (B013) for some years.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson leads the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and works on superconducting circuits at Chalmers, and flags possible recusal on circuit QED (B013); he states no conflict for B059.

Kroll spent a year in John Hall's laboratory, in the lineage in which Jun Ye worked, and leads quantum-sensing work in WACQT, a Chalmers-led centre; he flags the Hall-lineage connection to one proposed B059 laureate for the committee's judgement on recusal.
Olsson is an electron microscopist at Chalmers and says she should recuse herself from decisions on aberration-corrected TEM (B027).
Lindroth discloses general closeness to the atomic-theory community in B059 and past work with the Lund attosecond group, with no known connection to Katori or Ye.
Eriksson notes scientific proximity through 2D and van der Waals magnets to B034, with no personal or institutional tie.
Pearce (chair) works in astroparticle physics, which is the IceCube community's field, though not in IceCube, and flags the proximity; he has no institutional link to the B043 names.
questions_for_round2: For B059, is the lattice clock a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and can the citation state that distinction without depending on Ye's comb-related work?
For B059, does the primary record of 2003 to 2006 support Katori and Ye alone, or do Lemonde, Gill, Bloom or others have a claim that a two-name prize would unfairly ignore?
Should the pending redefinition of the second be treated as evidence of maturity for B059 or as a reason to wait?

For B034, is the existence of correlated and superconducting phases secure enough for a prize without a settled pairing mechanism, and is naming Jarillo-Herrero without Cao, Dean or others acceptable?
For B019, which three names, if any, can the committee defend among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and would the committee accept a collaboration discovery prize at all?
For B043, who was decisive among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers, and are TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 mature enough for the astrophysical interpretation?
For B016, does the 2016 topological-phases prize cover the Z2 topological insulator, and can Hasan and the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal be handled under the three-person cap?
Do Johansson's disclosed ties to circuit QED and Kroll's Hall-lineage connection require recusal on B013 or B059, and should outside reviewers assess B013 and B059 priority questions?
summary.chair_observation: After round 1 the explicit preferences are split: four members prefer B059 and one each prefers B034, B016, B019 and B043. B059 has the broadest explicit support and the simplest attribution, but its supporters ask for a primary-record check of priority and for a clear distinction from earlier prizes. The remaining first choices are each backed by one member and each carries a stated attribution or maturity reservation from the proposer, so round 2 should test those reservations rather than counts alone. As chair I note my own first choice (B043) and have stated its attribution and maturity issues in my round-1 file.
